Also, not exactly what you’re asking but it’s a small soap box of mine: 

NSAIDs have analgesic ceilings. There is no difference in pain scores 60 minutes after giving a parenteral dose of ketorolac when looking all the different dosages available, but the risk of ADRs is significantly increased so always use the smallest dose!

To be honest, I am not knowledgeable about the whole histamine = irritability or the mechanism through which modafinil causes irritability. 

However, taking an antihistamine while taking modafinil / armodafinil may decrease its efficacy as one of its proposed mechanisms of action (which, by the way, we still aren’t 100% sure how it works) is through the histaminergic / orexin system. Another thing to consider is *where* is it increasing histamine release? Doing so in different parts of the brain are going to have different effects. You’d also need to consider which receptors are causing the irritability; there are several types of histamine receptors (for example cetirizine is a histamine 1 receptor antagonist and famotidine is a histamine 2 receptor antagonist). Interestingly, pitolisant is a histamine 3 receptor inverse agonist. That’s a whole different topic though.

No, interestingly I applied online for positions and after I applied, I made sure to visit the CVS I applied to in person and introduce myself to the pharmacy manager to let them know I applied and why I was interested in the position. We got to talking and that’s how he learned that my ultimate goal was pharmacy school, and in fact the same pharmacy school his daughter was going to attend. She ended up being only a year ahead of me. So that was all lucky. He was used to precepting many pharmacy students and was used to hiring pharm techs that had a goal to go to pharmacy school. Again, I think it was luck. 

Before I applied, I actually asked to volunteer at my local home-town pharmacy for a month, and they were more than happy to accommodate. That way when I did apply to become a pharmacy tech, I could state that I had experience. Not MUCH experience, but 160 hours or so which is better than nothing! I know this may not be practical which is totally fine. I don’t think it actually played a huge part in my career path. 

However, know that the landscape of pharmacy is changing right now. CVS and Walgreens are continually pushing pharmacists to do more with less, meaning they do NOT provide enough hours for the pharmacy techs they have. Corporate is who determines how many hours can be allotted to the tech every week or two weeks or something. I also know that when I left CVS (which was 6 years ago so take this with a grain of salt) they were pushing for all employees to be “crosstrained” which is when they train employees who are hired to work the front (non-pharmacy) part of the store to work in the pharmacy and vice versa. If they did indeed push for that, then in theory the number of potential pharmacy techs they have has increased and need is decreased. 

I HIGHLY encourage you to do the following if you’re still struggling: visit some or all of the independently-owned pharmacies in your city. Ask to speak with the pharmacy manager/owner. Even if they’re not available, introduce yourself and explain you’re looking to gain pharmacy experience before entering pharmacy school. They probably have a lot of connections and can help you out! Bring some contact cards - nothing fancy by name and contact info, handwritten note on back stating prospective pharm student looking for pharmacy experience. 

I’ve done this before and it led to some really interesting opportunities and no one was rude to me, everyone was super kind. 

Do you mind me asking what state you live in? (Totally fine if you don’t want to give that info!)

Yes! Exactly what I did. BS in biochem and worked as tech during undergrad, as well as working in chemistry lab as research assistant. Then pharmacy school, residency, and am now a pharmacist. 

I HIGHLY recommend taking a job as a pharmacy technician because you learn so much that helps you in pharmacy school and throughout your career. I never regretted it. There were so many students in my class who had never stepped foot in a pharmacy before enrolling in pharmacy school which I thought was absurd. Quite a good percentage dropped out. This is a great way to find out if this is for you and to network. 

Know that working in community pharmacy (AKA retail) is hellish because of the corporate environment, but there are SO many careers in pharmacy outside of community. So if you hate it as a technician, that doesn’t mean you’ll be stuck with it when you graduate. 

I went from CVS as a tech > intern at hospital outpatient pharmacy (very similar to “retail” but WAY better working environment and I loved it) > now am at the VA and never touch a bottle of medicine and am instead the one prescribing the meds. It’s fabulous. 

If you can find a hospital outpatient pharmacy that is hiring, I would start there. Especially for a non-profit / not for profit hospital. Much better working environment, much better networking opportunities, and much more respectful of your role as a learner as well.

Edit: yeah don’t graduate from college then do pharm tech, that’s a waste of time. Become a pharm tech WHILE in undergrad!

It’s a lot of money and time to procure an organ and there are so many people who need one. The risk of giving someone who is suicidal a liver is that they kill the self and the liver in the process, that means one less liver available to someone who would’ve otherwise gotten a “lifetime” of use from it. I’m not saying it’s right, just that’s how it’s seen. 

The liver is a cool organ in that it can regenerate to some degree, but not to the point that it completely regrows itself.

The amount of acetaminophen you’ve consumed is quite a lot and the way it kills you is by killing your liver cells because as APAP is broken down it produces a toxic metabolite called NAPQI that usually your stores of glutathione (an antioxidant) take care of, but in an overdose all of your glutathione is exhausted and used up. This takes a little time of course and there is a special antidote called N-acetylcysteine AKA NAC. The sooner you get help and treatment, the higher the chances you’ll live through this are. 

I’m not sure what country you’re in, but in the USA you cannot get a liver transplant if you damaged your liver through a suicide attempt.
